query: In Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs phase stability and why, with relevance to retaining desirable combinations of high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness? Specify a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries of the hypothesis, supporting prior evidence, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys, the degree of local lattice distortion induced by atomic size mismatches—particularly modulated by Al content—governs phase stability by shifting the free-energy balance between FCC and BCC structures. This mechanism stabilizes a desirable microstructure that enables high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness.
generation.material_initial_state: An equiatomic or near equiatomic Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloy exhibiting a mixture of FCC and BCC phases with favorable mechanical and environmental properties.
generation.intervention: Controlled variation of the Al concentration (or a similar element with a larger atomic radius) while keeping other elemental ratios constant.
generation.conditions: Samples are prepared under identical processing conditions with only the Al concentration systematically varied within a narrow compositional window (e.g., ±5% relative to the equiatomic baseline). Measurements are performed at room temperature, high temperature, and cryogenic conditions, and under simulated radiation environments.
generation.structural_mediator: Magnitude of local lattice distortion (quantified, for example, by XRD peak broadening or EXAFS measurements) as induced by atomic size mismatch.
generation.mechanism: Increasing Al content increases atomic size mismatch, thereby raising the lattice distortion energy. This additional strain energy alters the free-energy landscape, favoring the stabilization of one phase (typically BCC) over a mixed or competing phase structure. The controlled phase evolution, via this lattice distortion, supports the retention of high-temperature strength, corrosion resistance, radiation tolerance, and toughness at cryogenic temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline equiatomic alloy, samples with moderately increased Al will display a measurable increase in lattice distortion and a shift toward a higher fraction of the BCC phase. This phase shift will correlate with changes in mechanical and environmental performance such that an optimal balance of properties is achieved before the onset of deleterious intermetallic precipitation.
generation.baseline: The equiatomic Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloy with a known balance of FCC and BCC phases exhibiting desirable high-temperature strength, corrosion resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to hold within a narrowly tuned compositional regime (small deviations around the equiatomic point); outside this boundary (large deviations in Al content or introduction of other elements that significantly alter atomic size mismatch), other mechanisms (e.g., chemical ordering or different thermodynamic factors) may dominate phase stability.
generation.uncertainty: While the link between increased lattice distortion from Al variation and phase stability is supported by general high-entropy alloy principles, the precise quantitative relationship and its impact on all targeted properties (especially the simultaneous optimization of high-temperature strength and cryogenic toughness) remain to be fully defined. Moreover, potential interactions with processing conditions and secondary phase precipitations add uncertainty to the exact behavior.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of high-entropy alloy samples with incremental Al adjustments around the equiatomic composition. Characterize the local lattice distortion using XRD and EXAFS, quantify phase fractions (FCC versus BCC) using TEM and diffraction, and measure mechanical properties (e.g., high-temperature strength, cryogenic toughness) as well as environmental and radiation resistance.
measurements: XRD peak broadening metrics to quantify lattice distortion
Mechanical property tests at high temperature and cryogenic temperatures
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no systematic correlation is observed between the degree of lattice distortion (as measured by peak broadening or local structure analysis) and the shift in phase fractions (or if phase stability does not change in the predicted manner with increasing Al content), or if the mechanical and environmental performance does not correlate with these structural changes, then the hypothesis that lattice distortion governs phase stability under these conditions would be falsified.
